§12.2.1 Blueprints

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

diagrams-blueprints · images diagrams

✅ Normative

A floor plan or architectural drawing MUST use a faithful diagram/<language> encoding, preferring diagram/tikz then diagram/svg. If no suitable language can represent it faithfully, it MUST use a fenced description block. The output MUST preserve visible geometry, labels and printed measurements without inferred relationships or computed values. It MUST NOT be a table.

Floor plans and architectural drawings.

How the element is recognised

A drawing whose content is spatial: walls, rooms, dimensions, door swings, labels placed where the thing they name sits. There are no rows and no columns — only positions.

Why a table is the wrong answer

A floor plan forced into a grid becomes a table of spatially adjacent labels that reads as data downstream. That is worse than a description, because it is confidently wrong: nothing in the output signals that the rows and columns were invented — the never invent failure. A floor plan MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

The same trap appears in Geographic Maps§12.2.4 (map coerced into a table) and Electrical Schematics§12.2.3 (circuit coerced into a graph): a spatial artefact flattened into a linear structure that cannot carry position.

Encode the spatial content

Language selection follows Diagrams and Flowcharts§12.2.2. The encoding MUST preserve visible walls, openings, door swings, relative positions, dimensions, labels, scale bars, legends and notes. Drawing coordinates MAY follow the visible geometry; they MUST NOT assert unprinted real-world measurements. Inconsistent printed dimensions MUST be copied without correction. A room graph that drops geometry is not a faithful encoding of a floor plan.

Description fallback

Only when no suitable language can faithfully encode the drawing, use a fenced description block in this shape:

  1. What it is — one line describing the drawing.
  2. Areas and visible structure — one item per labelled area in reading order, its printed label and size verbatim, followed by visible walls, openings and spatial relationships.
  3. Dimensions and notes — every dimension line, scale bar, legend entry, north arrow label and note, verbatim.

Unshown adjacency, hidden openings, computed areas and corrected dimensions MUST NOT be added. A visible doorway or shared wall may be described as drawn; proximity alone does not establish a connection. The description MUST distinguish what is visible from what cannot be determined.

✅ Sample — a single-storey plan

Twelve labelled areas, eight of them with a printed size, and dimension lines on all four sides. The printed dimensions do not add up (32'-0", 40'-0" and 44'-0" under a 62'-0" span) and are copied as printed.
